props.title: Cobb

sections.content: Cobb (1994) stands as one of cinema's most fascinating yet overlooked biopics about Hollywood legend Ty Cobb. Director Ron Shelton, fresh off Bull Durham (1988), strips away baseball mythology to reveal a racist, violent man whose demons followed him to his grave. Tommy Lee Jones delivers a savage performance that makes Raging Bull (1980) look tame by comparison. The film's genius lies in its framing device - having sportswriter Al Stump (Robert Wuhl) attempt to ghostwrite Cobb's sanitized autobiography while witnessing the baseball legend's true monstrous nature. This creates a compelling tension between myth-making and truth-telling that echoes later sports biopics like The Fighter (2010).

sections.content: What sets Cobb apart from standard sports biopics is its unflinching commitment to showing its subject's depravity. Unlike sanitized fare like 42 (2013) or Field of Dreams (1989), Shelton presents Cobb as an unredeemable figure whose baseball greatness came at a terrible human cost. The film shares DNA with darker sports character studies like The Wrestler (2008) and Foxcatcher (2014), examining how athletic excellence can mask deep psychological damage. Jones' performance captures both Cobb's physical deterioration and his paranoid rage at a changing world that no longer tolerates his bigotry and violence.

The film's structure brilliantly uses Stump's moral dilemma as its spine. Should he write the whitewashed version Cobb demands or reveal the ugly truth? This ethical wrestling match echoes through later journalism films like Frost/Nixon (2008) and The End of the Tour (2015). Shelton stages their interactions like psychological warfare, with Cobb alternating between charm and menace as he tries to control his legacy. The film becomes less about baseball than about power, truth, and America's need to create sporting heroes even at the cost of ignoring their monstrosity. SUBHEAD: Breaking Down Baseball Myths

sections.content: While most baseball films like A League of Their Own (1992) or The Sandlot (1993) trade in nostalgia, Cobb deliberately shatters those rose-colored glasses. Shelton, who played minor league baseball himself, understood how the sport's mythology often obscures uncomfortable truths about racism, greed, and corruption. The film pairs naturally with John Sayles' Eight Men Out (1988) in examining baseball's dark underbelly. Both films suggest that America's pastoral national pastime has always had poison at its roots.
